args.body:
STIPULATION MARKUP ANALYSIS AND RECOMMENDATIONS MEMO

TO: Client Leadership and Deal Team
FROM: Counsel
DATE: [Current Date]
RE: IRS Counterparty Markup of Proposed Stipulation of Facts – Carried Interest Tax Court Dispute

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The IRS has submitted a markup of our proposed Stipulation of Facts containing three material deviations from the base agreement. After reconciliation against the disclosure schedules and applicable precedent, we identify one walk-away issue requiring immediate escalation and two issues requiring negotiation. Client priorities have been updated per the latest deal correspondence, and this memo reflects the controlling instruction.

PRIORITY TIER 1: WALK-AWAY ISSUE

I. SURVIVAL PERIOD REDUCTION (Critical – Deal-Threatening)

Issue: The markup introduces a new limitation period that shortens survival for the core representations to an unacceptable threshold inconsistent with the survival matrix in Exhibit B.

Background & Analysis:
• Our base agreement establishes a survival period set forth in Exhibit B's comprehensive survival matrix for tax representations and indemnification obligations
• The IRS markup silently inserts a limitation-period provision that contradicts the scheduled survival periods
• This creates direct conflict with the scheduled exceptions, which control over general statements per the documents' hierarchy
• The core tax representations are fundamental to the case resolution and warrant full contractual protection

Regulatory & Precedential Context:
• In tax court stipulations, survival periods for representations typically extend 3-5 years post-closing to permit comprehensive audit review
• The IRS's compressed timeline appears designed to prematurely cut off discovery and indemnification rights
• This deviation materially increases our post-closing exposure to undisclosed tax liabilities

Client Position: Per the latest controlling instruction in the deal correspondence, the client treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue and will not concede this point.

RECOMMENDATION: Reject the survival-period limitation language entirely and insist on strict adherence to the Exhibit B survival matrix. Communicate to the IRS that this provision is non-negotiable and trigger escalation protocols if they refuse to remove it.

---

PRIORITY TIER 2: NEGOTIABLE ISSUES

II. MATERIAL ADVERSE EFFECT CARVE-OUTS (Material – Negotiable with Conditions)

Issue: The markup's revised definition of Material Adverse Effect adds regulatory action carve-outs that precisely target the types of regulatory matters at the core of this tax dispute.

Background & Analysis:
• Our base agreement contains standard MAC/MAE language protecting both parties against unforeseen circumstances
• The IRS markup inserts new carve-outs that exclude "regulatory action" from the definition of Material Adverse Effect
• Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that directly intersect these new carve-outs
• The result is that disclosed regulatory risks are now shielded from indemnification under the revised MAE definition

The Scheduling Conflict:
• Schedule 3.7 lists specific pending regulatory inquiries—these are disclosed items that constrain representations
• By adding a blanket regulatory action carve-out, the IRS attempts to use general language to undo the scheduled disclosures
• This creates an internally contradictory agreement: Schedule 3.7 narrows representations while the markup narrows remedies for breaches of those narrowed reps
• The controlling hierarchy is that scheduled exceptions trump general statements

Risk Assessment:
• If we accept the carve-outs, we accept that future regulatory action (even within the scope of the disclosed inquiries) will not trigger indemnification
• The IRS gains a de facto release from disclosed liabilities once the agreement closes
• We lose leverage in negotiating the scope of pending inquiry responses

RECOMMENDATION: Modify the MAE carve-out to explicitly exclude it from application to matters disclosed in Schedule 3.7 and to other regulatory inquiries specifically identified in the markup. Propose narrowing the carve-out to unforeseen regulatory action only, not to matters already under investigation or disclosed. If the IRS resists, escalate for strategic discussion regarding whether accepting a limited carve-out is worth the concession on the survival period (which we are unwilling to concede).

---

III. INDEMNIFICATION BASKET CONVERSION AND CAP REDUCTION (Moderate – Client Has Flexibility)

Issue: The markup silently reduces the indemnification cap and converts the basket from a deductible structure to a tipping basket, fundamentally altering loss-recovery mechanics.

Background & Analysis:
• Our base agreement establishes an indemnification cap and uses a traditional deductible basket (aggregate losses below the basket threshold are non-recoverable; above the threshold, all losses are recoverable)
• The IRS markup converts this to a tipping or reverse-breakpoint basket structure (losses don't accumulate toward a threshold; instead, the entire indemnification obligation is eliminated if claims fall below the tipping point)
• Simultaneously, the cap amount is reduced, limiting our overall recovery ceiling

Schedule 5.2 Impact:
• Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities—items we are responsible for post-closing, not the IRS
• The markup's indemnification changes would silently shift some of these retained liabilities by creating a lower cap and a more restrictive basket
• The scheduled items control: if Schedule 5.2 establishes that certain liabilities are "retained," the markup cannot use contractual mechanics to effectively shift responsibility

Financial & Operational Consequence:
• A deductible basket incentivizes both parties to manage costs below the threshold; we maintain some recovery even for smaller claims
• A tipping basket creates a cliff: if cumulative claims fall just below the tipping point, we recover nothing, incentivizing the other party to fragment claims
• The reduced cap on top of the tipping basket creates compounding loss of recovery protection

Market Practice & Precedent:
• Tax court stipulations and settlements typically use deductible baskets with caps set at 0.5%-2% of the amount in dispute
• The conversion to a tipping basket is non-standard and favors the counterparty's incentive to contest small claims

Client Position & Flexibility: Per the deal correspondence, the client will concede the basket conversion but does NOT wish to concede a survival-period reduction. This suggests the client has strategic flexibility on indemnification mechanics if necessary to preserve the survival period. However, the cap reduction should not be accepted without negotiation.

RECOMMENDATION: 
1. Accept the conversion from a deductible to a tipping basket only as part of a negotiated settlement that preserves the full Exhibit B survival matrix (our walk-away issue in Tier 1).
2. Push back on the cap reduction: request that the indemnification cap remain at its original level or be indexed to a defined percentage of disputed amounts.
3. If the IRS insists on a reduced cap, tie the reduction to a correspondingly extended survival period to maintain overall deal balance.
4. Document the Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities explicitly in the indemnification section to prevent the markup's contractual mechanics from shifting those liabilities.

---

RECONCILIATION OF SCHEDULES AGAINST MARKUP CHANGES

The schedules establish the controlling baseline for representations and liabilities:

• Schedule 3.7 (Pending Regulatory Inquiries): Controls the scope of disclosed regulatory matters that the MAE carve-out must respect. Any carved-out regulatory action must exclude items listed in Schedule 3.7.

• Schedule 5.2 (Retained Liabilities): Controls the allocation of responsibility post-closing. The indemnification changes cannot be used to effectively shift liabilities already scheduled as retained.

• Exhibit B (Survival Matrix): Controls the minimum duration for which representations survive and indemnification obligations remain enforceable. The markup's limitation period must conform to Exhibit B, not replace it.

---

INTEGRATED NEGOTIATION STRATEGY

Given the controlling client instruction that survival-period reduction is a walk-away issue, we recommend the following integrated approach:

1. Lead with Tier 1: Immediately reject the survival-period limitation and make clear this is non-negotiable. Provide the IRS with the Exhibit B reference and explain that the schedule controls the limitation period.

2. Address Tier 2 Conditionally: Acknowledge that we can discuss the MAE carve-outs and indemnification basket mechanics, but only in the context of a settlement that preserves the full Exhibit B survival matrix. Frame these items as negotiable only if the walk-away issue is resolved in our favor.

3. Document Schedule Supremacy: In all responses, emphasize that Schedule 3.7, Schedule 5.2, and Exhibit B are controlling baselines that general representations and remedies cannot override. This establishes a clear interpretive framework.

4. Escalation Path: If the IRS refuses to remove the survival-period limitation, recommend immediate escalation to client leadership and discuss whether alternative dispute resolution or settlement discussions are more efficient than continued negotiation over a non-negotiable point.

---

CONCLUSION

The IRS markup introduces three material deviations. The survival-period reduction is a deal-breaking issue requiring immediate rejection. The MAE carve-outs require negotiation but can be addressed through schedule-specific limitations. The indemnification changes are negotiable and can be conceded as part of a broader settlement, but only if the survival period is preserved. 

We recommend immediate communication to the IRS that the survival-period limitation is unacceptable and that further negotiation on indemnification and MAE issues depends on the IRS's willingness to conform the limitation period to the Exhibit B survival matrix.

---

APPENDIX: RECOMMENDED RESPONSE TO IRS MARKUP

Dear IRS Counsel:

We have reviewed your markup of the Proposed Stipulation of Facts and identified the following issues requiring resolution:

1. SURVIVAL PERIOD (Non-Negotiable): The new limitation-period provision contradicts Exhibit B's established survival matrix and is unacceptable. We require that this language be deleted entirely, and the agreement conform to the survival schedule as drafted. This is a material requirement and non-negotiable.

2. MATERIAL ADVERSE EFFECT (Negotiable): We can discuss the revised MAE definition, but any regulatory-action carve-outs must exclude matters disclosed in Schedule 3.7 and currently under investigation. We propose narrowing the carve-out to unforeseen regulatory developments only.

3. INDEMNIFICATION (Conditional): We are prepared to discuss the basket mechanics, provided that (a) the Exhibit B survival matrix is preserved in full, and (b) the indemnification cap is not reduced below [original amount or [X]% of disputed value].

We look forward to your response and suggest a call to discuss next steps.

Respectfully,
Counsel
